body.text: One hook, one strand of yarn and three stitches get you a surprising distance, and by Sunday you could be holding something you made. Crochet looks harder than it is, partly because a written pattern reads like code. This guide starts with the stitches, then walks you through a flat square.
Crochet uses a single hook where knitting uses two needles. The first row will be wonky. That's normal.

essentials: One crochet hook, in the size your yarn label suggests
A ball of smooth, medium-weight (worsted) yarn in a light, solid color
A blunt yarn needle for weaving in ends
optional: A few stitch markers, or safety pins, to mark the start of a row
A tote to carry it everywhere
A second hook in a different size to see how the stitches change

body.text: You probably own scissors and a bag already, and a friend may have a spare hook and half a ball of yarn. Light, solid-colored yarn shows each stitch clearly, which makes it a friendly choice for a first square; dark or variegated yarn can make stitches harder to see, so keep it for later. A hook with a comfortable handle is a lovely upgrade if your hand tires, and a few stitch markers make counting rows easier.

body.title: What to grab for your first square
body.dek: A hook and one plain ball of smooth, light yarn are all a first square needs. Pick the hook size your yarn label suggests.

body.text: The three stitches that open the door

body.title: The slip knot and the chain
body.note: Every project starts with a loop on the hook, then a row of chains pulled through one after another. It is the foundation of everything.

body.title: Single crochet
body.note: A short stitch that makes dense fabric, and the one the first square below uses.

body.title: Double crochet
body.note: A taller stitch, so rows grow faster. Try it once single crochet feels comfortable.

body.text: A heads-up before you follow any pattern: US and UK crochet terms differ. What US patterns call single crochet is double crochet in UK terms, and US double crochet is UK treble, so check which one a pattern uses. A pattern that says "sc" is written in US terms.
**What makes it easier:** a hook with a comfortable handle, so longer sessions stay pleasant when your hand tires.

items: Make a slip knot and slide it onto the hook, snug but not tight.
Chain 20, or about as wide as you want the square. Count as you go.
Skip the first chain next to the hook, then work a single crochet into each chain along the row.
Chain one, turn the work around, and work single crochet into each stitch of the previous row.
Count your stitches at the end of every row. If the number changes, the edges are drifting. A small practice swatch like this one catches tension and counting slips before they waste yarn.
Repeat until it is roughly square, then cut the yarn and pull the tail through the last loop.

body.text: Weave the ends in with the yarn needle. Check the yarn label before washing the finished piece, as care varies by fiber. A single row before dinner is a good first day, and if your hands ache, shake them out and stop. A relaxed grip also makes more even stitches.
**What makes it easier:** a few stitch markers or safety pins in a contrasting color, so the first stitch of each row is easy to find and your count stays right.

body.title: A comfortable hook, for when you want to keep going
body.dek: Hooks come in sets with a range of sizes and handles. A set lets you try the size your yarn label suggests, and then the next size up when a row feels tight.

body.text: A written pattern looks like code at first glance: ch 20, sc in 2nd ch from hook, turn. It's shorthand, and a pattern should list its abbreviations at the top. Read one line at a time with a finger under the part you are on, and do exactly what it says even when it seems odd. The sense arrives a few rows later.
The yarn label does quiet work too: it lists the weight, the suggested hook and care instructions. Keep a label in your project bag so you can match the yarn when you need more.
**Worth bringing:** a small project pouch or tote, so the hook, yarn, scissors and a yarn label for matching travel together.

Once a flat square feels easy, the natural next steps are a longer rectangle for a scarf, a handful of small squares to join into something bigger, or a simple round coaster. They're the same few stitches in a new arrangement.

items: **The edges keep growing or shrinking.** You are gaining or losing stitches at the turn. Count at the end of every row and mark the first stitch of each row.
**It's too tight to work.** Try a hook one size up and hold the yarn more loosely. Everyone grips too hard at first.
**A mistake three rows back.** Pull out the hook and gently unravel to the mistake. Redoing a row is part of the craft, not a failure.
